issues.legal_issue: A statutory declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive as to both the need and the public character of the purpose, except where the declaration is a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared that the land was needed for a public purpose, namely to establish a factory manufacturing refrigeration equipment.
The landowners challenged whether the acquisition was genuinely for a public purpose and argued that the declaration could not prevent judicial examination of that question.
The court found no basis on the record to treat the declaration as a colourable exercise of power.
issues.conclusion: The declaration was conclusive as to both the need for the land and whether the purpose was public, and the court could not examine those questions on their merits; a colourable exercise of power remained open to challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a declaration is conclusive evidence that land is needed for a public purpose or for a company. The court held that “conclusive evidence” has the same effect as “conclusive proof” under section 4 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872: once the prescribed evidence is produced, contrary evidence is excluded. Sections 4, 5A, 6(1) and 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act show that the declaration covers the need and the character of the purpose together. The exception is a declaration made through fraud or colourable use of the acquisition power. The court distinguished Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India because it did not concern a declaration protected by section 6(3), and distinguished R. L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh because that case concerned the court’s interpretation of the limits on acquisition for a company under Part VII.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and government_declared_public_need and not colourable_exercise

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.government_declared_public_need: The government formally declared that the land was needed for a stated public purpose.
predicates.colourable_exercise: The government used the acquisition power as a sham for a private purpose or for no purpose authorized by the acquisition power.

issues.definition: When a landowner challenges an acquisition, a government declaration of public need is not open to merits review if the acquisition is not a colourable exercise of power.

issues.legal_issue: Making the government's declaration of public need conclusive does not, in the circumstances of a pre-constitutional acquisition law, invalidate the acquisition under the constitutional property guarantee.
material_facts: The acquisition was undertaken under a law enacted before the Constitution came into force.
The landowners argued that the rule making the declaration conclusive violated constitutional protections relating to property and restrictions on fundamental rights.
The court relied on earlier decisions holding that the acquisition law was protected from the relevant constitutional challenge.
issues.conclusion: The statutory conclusiveness of the declaration did not infringe the Constitution, and the challenge based on the constitutional property guarantee failed.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on Article 31(5)(a) of the Constitution and held that the pre-constitutional Land Acquisition Act was protected to the extent established in earlier decisions. It followed State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji, Lilavati Bai v. State of Bombay, Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, and State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga. The court held that the conclusiveness rule in section 6(3) did not thereby infringe the Constitution.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.preconstitutional_acquisition_law_applie: The compulsory acquisition is carried out under a law enacted before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.government_declaration_is_conclusive: The applicable law makes the government's declaration of public need conclusive evidence of that need and purpose.

issues.definition: A conclusive government declaration is constitutionally valid in a land-acquisition challenge where the acquisition is under a pre-constitutional law to which that constitutional protection applies.

issues.legal_issue: A nominal government contribution towards acquisition costs is not automatically insufficient to make an acquisition one partly at public expense, but its adequacy depends on the circumstances and whether the contribution is genuine.
material_facts: The government declared that the acquisition was at public expense and later sanctioned a contribution towards the acquisition costs.
The contribution was nominal compared with the land's value and was sanctioned after the challenge had been filed.
The government said that the project had been considered at different levels and that a public contribution had been decided upon; that account was not challenged.
The court found no sufficient basis to infer that the government had decided not to contribute public funds or had used the contribution as a sham.
issues.conclusion: By majority, the nominal contribution did not invalidate the acquisition on these facts; a token contribution may suffice in a particular case, but it is not necessarily sufficient in every case. Subba Rao J. dissented, holding that the contribution had to be a substantial part and that the acquisition was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits compensation to be paid wholly or partly out of public revenues. The majority held that “partly” does not necessarily mean a substantial part and that adequacy depends on the facts; a nominal amount may nevertheless indicate colourable action in particular circumstances. The majority approved Sanja Naicken v. Secretary of State and Vedlapatla Suryanarayana v. Province of Madras, and disapproved Ponnaia v. Secretary of State. It held Chatterton v. Cave and Maharajah Luchmeswar Singh v. Chairman of the Darbhanga Municipality inapplicable. Subba Rao J., dissenting, adopted the substantial-part interpretation and relied on Ponnaia.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and government_committed_public_funds and stated_public_contribution_is_genuine and not colourable_exercise

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.government_committed_public_funds: The government undertook to pay some of the acquisition costs from public funds.
predicates.stated_public_contribution_is_genuine: The circumstances support that the government actually decided to contribute public funds, rather than merely announcing a sham contribution.
predicates.colourable_exercise: The government used the acquisition power as a sham for a private purpose or for no purpose authorized by the acquisition power.

issues.definition: A nominal public contribution is not automatically insufficient where the government genuinely undertook to contribute and the acquisition is not a colourable exercise of power.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition to establish a privately operated industry may be for a public purpose, rather than an acquisition for a company under the company-acquisition provisions, when the undertaking is found to benefit the community.
material_facts: The land was acquired to establish a factory manufacturing refrigeration compressors and ancillary equipment for a private enterprise.
The record described expected benefits including reduced imports, potential exports, employment, technical development, and support for food preservation and public utilities.
The government made a contribution towards acquisition costs, and the landowners did not establish that the stated public purpose was a sham.
The acquisition proceeded without compliance with Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was for a public purpose at public expense and was not invalid for failure to follow the company-acquisition procedure in Part VII.
issues.legal_principle: The court described a public purpose broadly as one in which the general interest of the community, rather than the particular interest of individuals, is directly and vitally concerned. It relied on the inclusive definition in section 2(f), and the scheme of sections 4, 6 and Part VII, including sections 40 and 41, of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It relied on Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay for the broad meaning of public purpose and distinguished R. L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which concerned the statutory limits on an acquisition expressly made for a company.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and private_industry_is_acquisition_beneficiary and undertaking_has_community_benefits and government_declared_public_need and not colourable_exercise

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.private_industry_is_acquisition_benefici: A private enterprise is to use the acquired land for its undertaking.
predicates.undertaking_has_community_benefits: The undertaking is expected to produce benefits extending beyond the private enterprise to the community.
predicates.government_declared_public_need: The government formally declared that the land was needed for a stated public purpose.
predicates.colourable_exercise: The government used the acquisition power as a sham for a private purpose or for no purpose authorized by the acquisition power.

issues.definition: An acquisition benefiting a private industry may proceed as a public-purpose acquisition without the company-acquisition procedure when the undertaking has community benefits, the government declared a public need, and the acquisition is not colourable.

issues.legal_issue: Choosing one industry over another does not, by itself, discriminate against a landowner when the government determines that the selected industry serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The landowners said they planned to establish a paper mill and argued that the government had discriminated by acquiring their land for a refrigeration-equipment factory instead.
Their proposed project lacked an authorization to establish the factory at the acquired site, and the authorization relied upon related to a different location.
The government stated that refrigeration equipment would serve needs including food preservation and the development of cold-storage facilities.
The court recognized that the government could set priorities among industries in light of the state's needs and existing facilities.
issues.conclusion: The selection of the refrigeration-equipment industry did not, by itself, violate Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Article 14 and held that the state may determine which industry should receive priority as a public-purpose undertaking, taking account of public needs and existing facilities. It held that discrimination did not arise merely because the government declared the establishment of one particular industry to be a public purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.competing_industrial_project_asserted: The landowner asserts that a different industrial project could use the land and also benefit the community.
predicates.government_selected_industry_for_public_: The government selected an industry in light of the public needs and facilities it considered relevant.

issues.definition: A landowner's competing industrial proposal does not alone establish unequal treatment where the government selected an industry in light of public needs.

issues.legal_issue: The preliminary acquisition notification and the final declaration may be published on the same day when urgency provisions dispense with the opportunity to object before the final declaration.
material_facts: The government invoked the urgency procedure and directed that the statutory objection process would not apply.
The preliminary notification and the final declaration were made on different dates but published in the same Gazette issue.
The preliminary notification preceded the final declaration.
issues.conclusion: Publishing both notifications in the same Gazette issue was not irregular because the objection process had been dispensed with under the urgency procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 5A, 6 and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern the sequence. Ordinarily, the objection process under section 5A intervenes between the preliminary notification and the section 6 declaration. Where the government validly directs under section 17(4) that section 5A will not apply, that intervening process is absent, and same-day publication is not irregular if the preliminary notification precedes the final declaration.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and urgency_procedure_invoked and objection_process_dispensed_with and preliminary_notification_preceded_final_declaration

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.urgency_procedure_invoked: The government invoked an urgency procedure for the acquisition.
predicates.objection_process_dispensed_with: The government directed that the usual opportunity to object before the final declaration would not apply.
predicates.preliminary_notification_preceded_final_: The preliminary notification was made before the final declaration, even if both were published on the same day.

issues.definition: Same-day publication is not irregular when urgency removes the intervening objection process and the preliminary notification was made before the final declaration.
